blocks.text: Land resources and land use

Any part of the environment that people value and can use to meet their needs, because technology and culture make it useful. Resources can be renewable (such as water and forests) or non-renewable (such as coal and petroleum).

Land is the basic resource, because farming, forests, towns and industries all depend on it. The **land use** of India is shown by the Land Use Statistics under nine headings:

1. Forests
2. Land put to non-agricultural uses (settlements, roads, industries)
3. Barren and wasteland (rocky, desert, hilly land that cannot be cultivated)
4. Permanent pasture and other grazing land
5. Land under miscellaneous tree crops and groves
6. Culturable wasteland (left uncultivated for more than five years)
7. Current fallow (left uncultivated for one year or less)
8. Fallow other than current fallow (left for one to five years)
9. **Net sown area** (the area sown with crops, counting an area sown more than once only once)

**Net sown area** is the largest single category of land in India. The area sown more than once in a year, added to the net sown area, is the **gross cropped area**. Forest area is less than the one-third of the land that the National Forest Policy aims at.
A cropping intensity of 100 per cent means that every hectare is sown once; a higher value means that part of the land is cropped more than once in a year.

What to learn from this figure: Net sown area counts each piece of land once, however many crops it grows. Gross cropped area counts every crop, so land sown twice is counted twice. The cropping intensity is the ratio of the two, and any value above 100 per cent means some land is cropped more than once in a year.

blocks.problem: A district has a net sown area of 8,000 hectares and a gross cropped area of 12,000 hectares. Find its cropping intensity and the area sown more than once.
blocks.solution: Cropping intensity is gross cropped area divided by net sown area, times 100, so it is 12,000 / 8,000 x 100 = 150 per cent. The area sown more than once is the gross cropped area minus the net sown area, which is 12,000 - 8,000 = 4,000 hectares. On average, every hectare of the net sown area is cropped one and a half times in the year.
blocks.answer: 150 per cent; 4,000 hectares sown more than once

blocks.text: Agriculture: major crops, development and problems

Indian agriculture has three cropping seasons. **Kharif** crops are sown with the onset of the south-west monsoon and harvested in autumn (rice, jowar, bajra, maize, cotton, jute, groundnut). **Rabi** crops are sown in winter and harvested in summer (wheat, barley, gram, mustard). **Zaid** crops are grown in the short period between rabi and kharif, mostly with irrigation (vegetables, melons, fodder).

What to learn from this figure: The seasons follow each other: kharif starts with the monsoon, rabi starts in winter, and zaid is the short irrigated gap between rabi and the next kharif. Link each season to its sowing trigger (monsoon, winter, irrigation) and to two or three crops.

rows: Sown with the onset of the south-west monsoon, harvested in autumn
Rice, jowar, bajra, maize, cotton, jute, groundnut
Sown in winter, harvested in summer

blocks.text:
Major crops:

- **Food grains**: rice (needs high temperature and heavy rainfall or irrigation), wheat (a cool-season crop of the north-western plains), and coarse grains or millets such as jowar, bajra and ragi.
- **Pulses**: gram, tur (arhar) and others, which fix nitrogen in the soil.
- **Oilseeds**: groundnut, mustard, sesame and soyabean.
- **Fibre crops**: cotton and jute.
- **Cash and plantation crops**: sugarcane, tea and coffee.

**Agricultural development** has meant increasing irrigation, the use of high-yielding seeds, fertilisers and machinery, as in the Green Revolution of the late 1960s, which raised wheat and rice production mainly in Punjab, Haryana and western Uttar Pradesh. **Problems of Indian agriculture**, as per NCERT, include:

- dependence on an uncertain monsoon and inadequate irrigation,
- low productivity in comparison with many countries,
- small and fragmented landholdings, so that mechanisation is difficult,
- shortage of credit, inputs and storage, and weak marketing,
- degradation of cultivated land through salinity, alkalinity and waterlogging,
- disguised unemployment and underemployment of the farm workforce.

Resources owned or managed collectively by a community and available to all its members, such as village pastures, community forests, village ponds and threshing grounds. Their use is regulated by the community, not by a single owner.

Common property resources matter greatly for the rural poor, who depend on them for fodder, fuelwood, water and minor forest produce. They are under stress from privatisation, encroachment and overuse.
Water resources: availability, utilisation and conservation

Water is available as surface water (rivers, lakes, ponds) and groundwater. India receives only about 4 per cent of the world's precipitation but has a far larger share of the world's people (as per NCERT), and the water is unevenly distributed in space and time because of the monsoon. Utilisation falls into: **irrigation** (by far the biggest user), **domestic use**, **industrial use** and other uses such as power generation and navigation. Irrigation takes the largest share, and the share of industries and domestic use is expected to rise as cities and industries grow.

**Scarcity of water** arises from three causes: growing population and rising demand; unequal distribution; and deterioration of quality because of pollution and over-extraction of groundwater, which lowers the water table. Water scarcity is felt in dry regions and also in cities.

**Conservation methods:**

- **Rainwater harvesting**: collecting and storing rain where it falls, or letting it sink into the ground to recharge groundwater. Examples are rooftop harvesting (compulsory in many cities, e.g. Tamil Nadu), tankas (underground tanks) and khadins and johads in Rajasthan, and bamboo drip irrigation in Meghalaya.
- **Watershed management**: the efficient management and conservation of surface and groundwater, together with soil and vegetation, within a drainage basin. Examples include the Haryali project of the central government, Neeru-Meeru (water and you) in Andhra Pradesh and the Arvari Pani Sansad in Alwar, Rajasthan.

What to learn from this figure: Rooftop harvesting collects rain where it falls. After filtering, the water can be stored for later use or allowed to sink through a recharge pit to refill groundwater. These are the two aims given in the lesson: storing rain, and recharging the groundwater.
$V$ volume of water harvested (m$^3$), $A$ roof area (m$^2$), $R$ rainfall (m), $c$ runoff coefficient (a fraction for losses). One cubic metre is 1,000 litres.

blocks.problem: A roof has an area of 100 square metres. The annual rainfall is 0.6 metre and the runoff coefficient is 0.8. How many litres of water can be harvested in a year?
blocks.solution: Use V = A x R x c. A = 100 m$^2$, R = 0.6 m and c = 0.8. So V = 100 x 0.6 x 0.8 = 48 cubic metres. Each cubic metre is 1,000 litres, so the water harvested is 48 x 1,000 = 48,000 litres a year. The runoff coefficient allows for losses by evaporation and splashing.

blocks.text: Mineral and energy resources

**Minerals** are classified as **metallic** and **non-metallic**. Metallic minerals are *ferrous* (containing iron: iron ore, manganese, chromite) and *non-ferrous* (without iron: bauxite, copper, lead, zinc, gold). Non-metallic minerals include mica, limestone, gypsum and dolomite. Mineral fuels such as coal and petroleum are the sources of energy.

What to learn from this figure: Classify in two steps: first metallic or non-metallic, then, for metals, ferrous (contain iron) or non-ferrous (no iron). Bauxite and copper are non-ferrous, so they are metallic but not ferrous. Coal and petroleum are mineral fuels and are the sources of energy.

blocks.caption: Main minerals and their distribution (as per NCERT)
rows: Damodar valley (Jharia, Raniganj, Bokaro), Godavari, Mahanadi and Son valleys

blocks.text: **Energy sources** are of two types. **Conventional sources** are those that have been used for long and are mostly exhaustible: firewood, cattle dung cake, coal, petroleum, natural gas and electricity (from hydro and thermal power). **Non-conventional sources** include nuclear energy (from uranium and thorium), solar, wind, tidal, geothermal, biogas and biomass energy. Most non-conventional sources are renewable and less polluting, and they are being promoted to reduce dependence on fossil fuels. Wind energy is important in Tamil Nadu and Gujarat, and geothermal energy has been explored at Manikaran in Himachal Pradesh and in the Puga valley of Ladakh.

What to learn from this figure: Conventional sources have been used for long and are mostly exhaustible. Non-conventional sources are mostly renewable and less polluting, which is why they are promoted. Use the word mostly: for example, nuclear energy is listed under non-conventional but is not a renewable source.
Planning in India: target area planning and sustainable development

India chose planned development after independence. The Planning Commission was set up in 1950, and five-year plans followed; in 2015 it was replaced by NITI Aayog. Early planning was **sectoral** (for agriculture, industry and so on). Later, uneven regional development led to **target area planning**, which gives special programmes to areas with particular problems, and **target group planning**.

**Target area planning** examples are the Command Area Development Programme, the Drought Prone Area Programme and the Hill Area Development Programme. The case study from NCERT is the **Bharmaur region of Himachal Pradesh**, a tribal area of the Gaddi people. An Integrated Tribal Development Project from the mid-1970s improved roads, schools, health services and irrigation, reducing the isolation and backwardness of this hilly area.

**Sustainable development** means development that meets the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs (the Brundtland Commission definition of 1987). The NCERT case study is the **Indira Gandhi Canal Command Area**. The canal begins at the Harike barrage, at the confluence of the Sutlej and Beas, and carries water to the dry areas of western Rajasthan up to Jaisalmer. Problems that appeared include waterlogging and salinity of the soil. The sustainability measures suggested are: lining of canals to stop seepage; avoiding water-intensive crops such as rice, sugarcane and cotton; afforestation and shelter-belt plantation; and pasture development.

What to learn from this figure: This case study follows a pattern you can reuse: an irrigation canal brought water to a dry region, problems (waterlogging and salinity) appeared, and sustainable-development measures were suggested. Learn the four measures as one list, since they are the usual answer to a question on sustainable development in this area.

Remember the keywords: net sown area is not the same as gross cropped area; watershed management covers land, water and vegetation together; and sustainable development is about the future generations. In map or case questions, name the place and the problem it solves.

Land use (nine categories); crops by season (kharif, rabi, zaid); CPRs are community-owned; rainwater harvesting and watershed management conserve water; coal in the Damodar valley; conventional vs non-conventional energy; Bharmaur (target area) and the Indira Gandhi Canal area (sustainable development).

diagrams.alt: Ten plots of land each sown once, four of them sown a second time, giving a net sown area of 10, gross cropped area of 14 and a cropping intensity of 140 per cent (illustrative numbers)
diagrams.caption: Net sown area, gross cropped area and cropping intensity (illustrative)
diagrams.description: Ten green plots are drawn in two rows. Each plot is marked crop 1, so each is sown once. Four of the plots also carry an amber box marked crop 2, meaning they are sown a second time in the year. A panel reads: net sown area is 10 plots, each counted once; area sown more than once is 4 plots; gross cropped area is 10 plus 4, which is 14 plots. Below, the rule cropping intensity equals gross cropped area divided by net sown area times 100 gives 14 over 10 times 100, which is 140 per cent. The numbers are illustrative only.

diagrams.alt: Three staggered bars in time order for the kharif, rabi and zaid cropping seasons with their sowing and harvest timing and example crops
diagrams.caption: Kharif, rabi and zaid cropping seasons in order (schematic)
diagrams.description: Three horizontal bars are placed one below another along a time arrow, so that their left-to-right position shows order in the year. Kharif, the first bar: sown at the onset of the south-west monsoon and harvested in autumn; crops include rice, jowar, bajra, maize, cotton, jute and groundnut. Rabi, the second bar, starting later: sown in winter and harvested in summer; crops include wheat, barley, gram and mustard. Zaid, the short third bar after rabi: the short period between rabi and kharif, mostly irrigated; crops include vegetables, melons and fodder. A note says bar position shows order, not exact months.

diagrams.alt: Schematic cross-section of rooftop rainwater harvesting: rain falls on a roof, runs through a gutter and down pipe to a filter, then to a storage tank or to a recharge pit that reaches the water table
diagrams.caption: Rooftop rainwater harvesting: store the water or recharge groundwater (schematic cross-section)
diagrams.description: A cross-section shows a house above ground level with rain falling on its roof. A blue roof gutter and down pipe carry the water down into the ground to a filter. From the filter a pipe leads to a junction with two branches: one to a storage tank labelled use later, and one to a recharge pit filled with gravel-like stones whose base reaches a dashed line labelled water table, with an arrow showing that groundwater is recharged. A note says the drawing is a schematic cross-section and not to scale.

questions.stem: Wheat is mainly grown in which cropping season of India?
questions.explanation: Wheat is sown in winter and harvested in spring or early summer, which makes it a rabi crop. Kharif crops are sown with the monsoon, and zaid crops are grown in the short season between rabi and kharif.

optionRationale.2: Kharif crops are sown at the onset of the monsoon, as rice is.
optionRationale.3: Zaid crops are grown between rabi and kharif.
optionRationale.4: Wheat is not grown equally in all three seasons.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a non-conventional source of energy?
questions.explanation: Solar, wind, tidal, geothermal, biogas and nuclear energy are non-conventional sources, and solar energy is the one listed here. Coal, petroleum and firewood are conventional sources that have been used for a long time.

optionRationale.4: Firewood is a traditional, conventional source.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a common property resource?
questions.explanation: Common property resources, such as village pastures, community forests and ponds, are used collectively by a community. A private farm, a factory or a household tank has a single owner.

optionRationale.1: A private farm belongs to its owner.
optionRationale.3: A factory is private or corporate property.
optionRationale.4: A household tank belongs to the household.

questions.stem: Iron ore is classified as a
questions.explanation: Iron ore contains iron and yields a metal, so it is a ferrous metallic mineral. Non-ferrous minerals do not contain iron, non-metallic minerals include mica and limestone, and mineral fuels include coal and petroleum.

optionRationale.1: Non-ferrous minerals do not contain iron.
optionRationale.3: Mineral fuels, such as coal, are burnt for energy.

questions.stem: A district has a net sown area of 8,000 hectares and a gross cropped area of 12,000 hectares. What is its cropping intensity?
questions.explanation: Cropping intensity is gross cropped area divided by net sown area, times 100 = 12,000 / 8,000 x 100 = 150 per cent. The inverse (8,000 / 12,000) gives about 67 per cent, which is not the intensity.

optionRationale.1: 67 per cent is the inverse ratio.
optionRationale.2: 120 per cent does not follow from the data.
optionRationale.4: 33 per cent is the share of the area sown more than once in the gross cropped area.

questions.stem: Match List-I (mineral or fuel) with List-II (a producing area as per NCERT).
questions.explanation: Raniganj in the Damodar valley produces coal (III), Digboi in Assam produces petroleum (I), Khetri in Rajasthan produces copper (IV) and Bailadila in Chhattisgarh produces iron ore (II). So the correct code is A-III, B-I, C-IV, D-II.

optionRationale.1: This swaps coal with Digboi and copper with Bailadila.
optionRationale.3: This reverses the correct pairing for most items.
optionRationale.4: This swaps petroleum with Bailadila and iron ore with Digboi.

questions.stem:
Assertion (A): Rainwater harvesting helps to recharge groundwater.
Reason (R): The rain collected is stored or guided into the ground through pits and wells instead of flowing away.
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
questions.explanation: Methods such as recharge pits, wells and ponds capture runoff and let it percolate to the water table. This is why harvesting raises the groundwater level, so (R) correctly explains (A).

optionRationale.2: Option 2 is wrong because (R) explains how recharge occurs.
optionRationale.3: Option 3 is wrong because (R) is true.
optionRationale.4: Option 4 is wrong because (A) is true.

questions.stem:
Consider the following about cropping seasons in India.
A. Kharif crops are sown with the onset of the monsoon.
B. Rabi crops are sown in winter and harvested in summer.
C. Zaid crops are grown in the short season between rabi and kharif.
D. Kharif crops need no water at all.
Which statements are correct?
questions.explanation: Kharif crops follow the monsoon, rabi crops are sown in winter and harvested in summer, and zaid crops fill the gap between them. Statement D is false because kharif crops such as rice need a great deal of water.

optionRationale.1: Option 1 omits C, which is also correct.
optionRationale.2: Option 2 omits A, which is also correct.
optionRationale.3: Option 3 includes the false statement D.

questions.stem: In the context of water conservation, watershed management refers to
options: storing water only in rooftop tanks
the integrated management of land, water and vegetation within a drainage basin
questions.explanation: A watershed is a drainage basin. Watershed management means managing and conserving soil, surface water, groundwater and vegetation together within the whole basin, as in the Haryali and Neeru-Meeru projects, and it is wider than any single storage method.

optionRationale.1: Rooftop tanks are one method of rainwater harvesting only.
optionRationale.2: Dams are one possible structure but not the definition.
optionRationale.4: Piped supply is a form of water distribution.

questions.stem: A roof of 100 square metres receives annual rainfall of 0.6 metre and the runoff coefficient is 0.8. How much water can be harvested in a year?
questions.explanation: The volume is area x rainfall x runoff coefficient = 100 x 0.6 x 0.8 = 48 cubic metres, which is 48,000 litres. Ignoring the runoff coefficient would give 60,000 litres, which is more than the roof can actually deliver.

optionRationale.2: 60,000 litres ignores the losses given by the runoff coefficient.
optionRationale.3: 4,800 litres is a slip of a factor of ten.
optionRationale.4: 80,000 litres does not follow from the data.

questions.stem: A district has a reporting area of 50,000 hectares. Forests cover 8,000, non-agricultural uses 6,000, barren land 4,000, all fallow land 5,000, and pasture, groves and culturable waste together 3,000 hectares. If the remainder is the net sown area and its cropping intensity is 140 per cent, what is the gross cropped area?
questions.explanation: The area under other uses is 8,000 + 6,000 + 4,000 + 5,000 + 3,000 = 26,000 hectares, so the net sown area is 50,000 - 26,000 = 24,000 hectares. Gross cropped area = net sown area x intensity = 24,000 x 1.4 = 33,600 hectares.

optionRationale.1: 24,000 hectares is the net sown area only.
optionRationale.3: 12,000 hectares has no basis in the data.
optionRationale.4: 30,000 hectares does not follow from 140 per cent.

questions.objective: Derive net sown and gross cropped areas from land use data

questions.stem:
Assertion (A): Under the sustainable plan for the Indira Gandhi Canal Command Area, water-intensive crops such as rice, sugarcane and cotton are encouraged.
Reason (R): Excess irrigation in the area has caused waterlogging and soil salinity.
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
questions.explanation: The plan avoids water-intensive crops and promotes shelter belts, afforestation and canal lining, so (A) is false. (R) is true, since excess irrigation has caused waterlogging and salinity, which is why those crops are avoided.

optionRationale.1: Option 1 is wrong because (A) is false.
optionRationale.2: Option 2 is wrong because (A) is false.
optionRationale.3: Option 3 is wrong because (R) is true.

questions.objective: Explain sustainable development measures in a command area

questions.stem:
Consider the following about energy sources.
A. Coal, petroleum and natural gas are conventional sources.
B. Solar, wind and biogas are non-conventional sources.
C. Most non-conventional sources are renewable and less polluting.
D. Natural gas is a renewable non-conventional source.
Which statements are correct?
questions.explanation: Coal, petroleum and natural gas are exhaustible conventional sources. Solar, wind and biogas are non-conventional, and most non-conventional sources are renewable and cleaner. Statement D is false because natural gas is a fossil fuel and a conventional source.

optionRationale.1: Option 1 omits C, which is also correct.
optionRationale.2: Option 2 includes the false statement D.
optionRationale.4: Option 4 includes the false statement D.

questions.stem: A district has a reporting area of 10,000 hectares, of which 70 per cent is net sown area. If 60 per cent of the net sown area is irrigated, how many hectares of the net sown area are unirrigated?
questions.explanation: Net sown area = 70 per cent of 10,000 = 7,000 hectares. Irrigated area = 60 per cent of 7,000 = 4,200 hectares. Unirrigated area = 7,000 - 4,200 = 2,800 hectares, which is 40 per cent of the net sown area.

optionRationale.2: 3,000 hectares is 30 per cent of the reporting area, not the unirrigated net sown area.
optionRationale.3: 1,200 hectares does not follow from the data.

questions.stem: Which of the following best illustrates the idea of sustainable development?
options: Pumping groundwater as fast as possible to raise output today
Using groundwater at a rate no faster than it is recharged, so that it remains available for future generations
Clearing all forests to expand farmland
Growing only water-intensive crops in a desert region
questions.explanation: Sustainable development meets the needs of the present without compromising the needs of future generations. Using groundwater no faster than the rate of recharge keeps the resource available. The other options exhaust a resource or damage the environment.

optionRationale.1: Rapid pumping depletes groundwater and harms the future.
optionRationale.3: Clearing all forests damages soil and climate and cannot last.
optionRationale.4: Water-intensive crops in a desert cause waterlogging and scarcity.

questions.objective: Apply the concept of sustainable development
